name: Hitman
summary: Hitman is a web app, apparently being reworked under the product name ALTER EGO, that helps sports fans make and review decisions about moments in matches. Cricket (especially the Indian Premier League) is the most developed sport, with smaller or pending support for football, Formula 1, tennis and basketball. Fans look at a match moment in the Decision Lab, lock in a call with a confidence level, and later see a grade, a rating and a personal Notebook. The app also has private friend groups called crews, a fantasy team builder, live cricket scores, and AI analyst characters whose wording is checked against verified facts. It is built with Next.js, a PostgreSQL database and Prisma, and it is careful about data licences, honest labelling and a strict no-money stance.
who_its_for: Sports fans, mainly cricket fans, who want to test and improve their reading of the game with friends. It is also for the developers and reviewers who maintain it.
how_it_runs: It is a Next.js web app that talks to a PostgreSQL database; a local database can be started with Docker or a built-in copy using the setup scripts. Automatic checks run on GitHub for pull requests, and a separate scheduled job downloads open sports data. Production hosting details are unclear from the summaries.

areas.name: tests
areas.summary: Browser tests, unit tests and a layering check that cover accessibility, sign-up, crews, the Lab, the Notebook, legal pages, the no-money rule and the maths behind calibration and grading. Deliberately broken sample files check that the architecture test works.
areas.why: They protect the product's promises about honesty, privacy and correctness.
areas.debug_tips: Find the test named after the feature that broke and read its failure message first. Database tests need the test database from the setup step.

areas.name: src/app
areas.summary: The pages and server endpoints users reach: home, login, Lab, Notebook, Alter Ego, crews, Desk, Rooms, Roster, legal pages, admin scoreboards and the API routes behind them.
areas.why: This is what people actually see and click.
areas.debug_tips: For a broken page, open its page.tsx. For a failing action, open the matching route.ts under api. The pages here mostly call the domain layer.

areas.name: src/domain
areas.summary: The business rules, grouped by topic such as accounts, crews, the Lab, contests, scoring, moderation and sources, usually as a service, a repo for database access and a types file.
areas.why: It holds the rules that decide what is allowed and what is shown.
areas.debug_tips: Wrong behaviour is usually in a service.ts, and wrong stored data in the matching repo.ts. Validation errors usually trace to types.ts.

areas.name: scripts
areas.summary: Command-line tools to download Cricsheet cricket data, load it into the database, fit and check the prediction models, pick the fifty golden moments, and measure performance or take screenshots.
areas.why: They produce the data and model files the app relies on.
areas.debug_tips: Check that the earlier step in the pipeline ran, such as download before ingest before fit. Many scripts need the environment settings loaded by with-env.mjs.

areas.name: src/ui
areas.summary: Shared visual building blocks such as the call ticket, receipt drawer, badges, charts and the central colour and size definitions.
areas.why: It keeps the look and honest data labels consistent everywhere.
areas.debug_tips: For wrong colours or sizes, look at tokens.css. For a mislabelled or missing badge, look at the matching file in components.

areas.name: src/engine
areas.summary: The calculation code: win probability for cricket chases, grading of picks, calibration, rating, Alter Ego personas, anti-cheat checks and simple models for basketball, tennis and F1.
areas.why: These numbers drive grades, ratings and every probability the user sees.
areas.debug_tips: Wrong numbers point here, so reproduce with the matching unit test under tests/unit/engine. Check overs handling in legalBalls.ts first for cricket oddities.

areas.name: prisma
areas.summary: The database definition and migrations for the Prisma tool. No file summaries for this folder were provided, so its contents are unclear.
areas.why: The database structure is defined here, though I cannot confirm details from the summaries.
areas.debug_tips: If tables or columns seem missing, the migrations probably have not been applied. The summaries do not say how to run them.

areas.name: src/providers
areas.summary: Shared plumbing: environment checks, logging, caching, rate limits, sign-in lookup, admin checks, language lookup, the choice of AI model and the data-rights helper.
areas.why: Other layers rely on it for safe, consistent basics.
areas.debug_tips: If the server refuses to start, check env.ts and the settings file. Too many requests errors come from rateLimit.ts.

areas.name: src/components
areas.summary: Larger interface pieces used across pages: the navigation bar, app frame, language toggle, live cricket score panels, team builder and landing page parts.
areas.why: They make up the common frame and the cricket and fantasy screens.
areas.debug_tips: For score panels, check LiveMatchCenter.tsx and the live-score route. For the team builder, check TeamBuilderClient.tsx and the fantasy rules file.

areas.name: src/llm
areas.summary: The layer that lets AI write analysis safely: it builds the input, calls Gemini, checks every claim against verified facts and banned words, and falls back to plain templates if anything fails.
areas.why: It is what keeps AI wording honest.
areas.debug_tips: If text looks generic, the verifier probably rejected the model and the template was used. Check verifier.ts and verified.ts.

areas.name: (root files)
areas.summary: Project-level setup: package list, Next.js and test configuration, the example settings file, the local database definition, setup and check scripts, GitHub workflows, research pages and the offline service worker.
areas.why: They control how the project is installed, checked and run.
areas.debug_tips: For build or install trouble, start with package.json, .env.example and harness/verify.mjs. For failing automatic checks, read the files under .github/workflows.

areas.name: Everything else
areas.summary: Supporting folders for data adapters (Cricsheet, OpenF1, StatsBomb), the licence check, AI persona cards, language text, landing wording and shared helper libraries such as sign-in and fantasy scoring.
areas.why: They feed clean, licensed data and shared helpers to the rest of the app.
areas.debug_tips: For missing or odd match data, check the adapter for that source. For blocked content, check src/rights/index.ts.

readiness.summary: Top fixes: add logging and error tracking with alerts, write a deploy and rollback runbook with a backup plan, and run the tests, dependency audit and a git history secret scan to confirm the unchecked areas.

checks.question: Does the app build and start with one documented command?
checks.evidence: `README.md` documents `node harness/init.mjs` then `npm run dev`, plus a Codespace path, and `package.json` has dev/build/start scripts. This is two commands rather than one, and none were run.
checks.next_step: Add a single `npm run setup` or `make start` that chains init and dev, and confirm it works on a clean clone.

checks.question: Are there automated tests, and do they pass?
checks.evidence: Not checked: tests were not run in this pass. 111 test files exist (unit in `tests/`, e2e in `tests/e2e/`, architecture and audit checks) with vitest coverage and Playwright, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` exists.
checks.next_step: Run `npm test` and `npm run test:e2e` and confirm the latest CI run is green.

checks.question: When something goes wrong, does the app show a clear message instead of crashing or failing silently?
checks.evidence: Not checked: user-facing error behavior needs a running app. Static scan found 1 swallowed-error match in 1 file, which is small but not yet reviewed.
checks.next_step: Review the swallowed-error match and confirm error boundaries and API error responses show clear messages.

checks.question: Does it check what people type or upload before using it?
checks.evidence: Input validation patterns appear in 28 matches across 16 files, which suggests validation on some routes. Coverage across all inputs and uploads is not shown.
checks.next_step: List every API route and form handler and confirm each parses input through a schema.

checks.question: Are passwords and API keys kept out of the code and out of git history?
checks.evidence: Only `.env.example` is tracked, `.gitignore` mentions `.env`, and a HEAD scan found 0 secret-like strings. Git history was not scanned.
checks.next_step: Run a history scan (gitleaks or trufflehog) and rotate anything found.

checks.question: Can only the right people see and change things (sign-in and permissions)?
checks.evidence: Auth, session and permission code shows 84 matches across 28 files, so access control exists. Whether every route and data mutation enforces it is not verified.
checks.next_step: Audit each route and server action for an auth and ownership check, and add tests for cross-user access.

checks.question: Is important data backed up, and are database changes made through migrations?
checks.evidence: Prisma migrations exist in `prisma/migrations` (init, one team per user per match, scoring ledger) and `db:migrate` uses `prisma migrate deploy`. No backup or restore plan is visible.
checks.next_step: Document backups and a restore test for the production Postgres in a runbook.

checks.question: Are third-party packages reasonably up to date and free of known security problems?
checks.evidence: Not checked: the dependency audit was not run. `package-lock.json` is committed, which makes versions reproducible.
checks.next_step: Run `npm audit` and `npm outdated`, and consider enabling Dependabot.

checks.question: If it breaks while people use it, will logs or alerts show what happened?
checks.evidence: Only 2 logging matches in 2 files, and no alerting or error-tracking setup is visible in the evidence.
checks.next_step: Add structured logging for server errors and connect an error tracker such as Sentry with an alert.

checks.question: Does it stay fast with realistic amounts of data and users?
checks.evidence: A `perf` script (`scripts/perf.mjs`) measures `/`, `/desk` and `/lab`, which shows performance is considered. No results or load testing with realistic data are shown.
checks.next_step: Run the perf script against seeded data and record budgets in CI.

checks.question: Is there a written, repeatable way to deploy it and to roll back a bad release?
checks.evidence: `vercel.json`, `docker-compose.yml` and CI workflows exist. No written deploy or rollback procedure is visible in the listed docs. `CHANGES.md` mentions manual steps still outstanding.
checks.next_step: Write `docs/DEPLOY.md` covering deploy, migration order and rollback (Vercel promote previous deployment, migration down plan).

checks.question: Could someone new run it and understand it from the docs alone?
checks.evidence: `README.md` gives run steps, a Codespace link and a verify command. `AGENTS.md`, `docs/TESTING.md` and `.agents/rules/` provide a project map and rules.

readiness.method: Static evidence only; tests, build and audit were not run in this pass.

debug_playbook.symptom: The app will not start or complains about settings
steps: Compare your local settings file with .env.example and fill in any missing values.
Check that the database is running using the db-up script or Docker.
Restart the app and read the first error message.

debug_playbook.symptom: A probability, grade or rating looks wrong
steps: Run the matching unit test and see if it fails.
Check overs handling, since 10.4 means ten overs and four balls.
Look for the provisional calibration badge, which signals a known calibration issue.

debug_playbook.symptom: Locking a call or opening a review fails
steps: Check that the user is signed in and has not hit the 20 locks per minute limit.
Check whether the anti-cheat rule refused a lock after the ball was bowled.
Read the lab service for the rule that rejected the request.

debug_playbook.symptom: Match data or the golden moments are missing
steps: Confirm the Cricsheet download ran and filled the raw data folder.
Run the ingest and seed steps against a running database.
Re-run the golden moments selection and check its output file.

debug_playbook.symptom: AI analyst text looks plain or generic
steps: Check whether Gemini is configured, since without it the app uses templates.
See if the verifier rejected the model's claims and triggered the fallback.
Look at the logged model call details on the admin scoreboards page.

glossary.meaning: The part of the app where a fan sees a match moment and locks in a call before the outcome is revealed.
A saved set of fifty high-impact IPL chase moments used in the Lab.
A private group of friends with an invite code, standings and a leaderboard.
A chess-style skill score for how well a fan reads decisions.
Checking that stated chances match what really happens, such as 70 percent calls being right about 70 percent of the time.
A drawer showing where a number came from, including its source and attribution.
A style profile and AI analyst persona given to a fan after ten graded calls.
A page of ranked, verified sports items offered in English and Hindi at three levels of detail.
An open source of ball-by-ball cricket match data used by the app.
Code that converts one outside data source into the app's common match format.
